slides.0.title: Hungary's Major Red Grape Varieties
slides.0.subtitle: Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Cabernet Franc and Others
slides.1.title: Kékfrankos — Hungary's Most Important Red Grape
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The Most Widely Planted Nationally
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Over 8,000 hectares — Hungary's most extensively planted red grape variety, and the same variety as Austria's Blaufränkisch
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The Backbone of Bull's Blood
slides.1.highlights.1.content: One of the principal varieties in the Bikavér (Bull's Blood) blends of Eger and Szekszárd
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Flavour Profile
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Black cherry, blueberry, violet, spice, high acidity, moderate tannins — with a refreshing, vibrant character
slides.1.highlights.3.title: International Persona
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Known as Blaufränkisch in Austria and Lemberger in Germany; Hungary's Sopron region produces the style closest to the Austrian expression
slides.1.content:
Kékfrankos is Hungary's national red variety — versatile, expressive and capable of producing wines ranging from fresh and aromatic to powerful and age-worthy, depending on the region and winemaking approach.

Aliases: Blaufränkisch (Austria) · Lemberger (Germany)
Ripening: Mid to late season
Key regions: Sopron · Eger · Szekszárd · Villány
Total planted: 8,000+ hectares

Regional Style Differences

Sopron: Light, elegant — the style closest to Austrian Blaufränkisch
Eger: Bikavér backbone — structured, spicy
Szekszárd: Rich, dark fruit, ripe tannins
Villány: Most concentrated — fully ripe, capable of single-variety quality
slides.2.title: Kadarka — The Soul of Traditional Bull's Blood
slides.2.highlights.0.title: An Ancient Native Variety
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Originally from the Balkans, Kadarka entered Hungary during the Ottoman occupation of the 16th century and was once the country's most important red grape
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Dramatically Reduced Plantings
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Sensitive to spring frosts and prone to inconsistent yields, Kadarka was largely replaced by Kékfrankos in the communist era — fewer than 700 hectares remain today
slides.2.highlights.2.title: A Distinctive Style
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Low tannins, deep red colour, with aromas of rose water, spice and dried wild strawberry — the "fragrant one" in any Bull's Blood blend
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Modern Revival
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Boutique winemakers are rediscovering Kadarka's charm, releasing single-variety bottlings that showcase its unique personality
slides.2.content:
Kadarka has a long and storied history in Hungary. Having arrived during the Ottoman period, it dominated Hungarian red wine production for centuries before falling victim to communist-era collectivisation.

🐂 The Legend of Bull's Blood

In 1552, during the Ottoman siege of Eger, Hungarian soldiers drank wine (mainly Kadarka-based Bikavér) to boost their courage. The red wine stained their beards, and when the Ottomans saw it, they believed the soldiers were drinking bull's blood — and retreated in fear. This colourful legend gave the wine its enduring name.

Today Kadarka is cultivated mainly in Szekszárd and Eger, where it remains an indispensable aromatic soul of any authentic Bikavér blend. Its low tannins and rose-spice fragrance provide a dimension that no other variety can replicate.
slides.3.title: Cabernet Franc — Villány's Ace Card
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Finding Its Home in Villány
slides.3.highlights.0.content: British wine critic Michael Broadbent once said: "Cabernet Franc has found its natural home in Villány"
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Hungary's Warmest Wine Region
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Villány's average annual temperature is close to that of southern France, allowing Cabernet Franc to ripen fully — without the herbaceous greenness sometimes found in the Loire Valley
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Top Quality Performance
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Villányi Franc is the only Hungarian wine with its own dedicated AOC brand, subject to strict quality controls
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Flavour Profile
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Ripe dark fruits (blackcurrant, damson), violet, pencil lead, cigar box — silky tannins and high ageing complexity
slides.3.content:
Cabernet Franc has found its Hungarian "hero's stage" in Villány, Hungary's southernmost and warmest wine region. Here the variety achieves a level of ripeness and complexity that rivals the Right Bank of Bordeaux.

Latitude: 45.8°N
Average temperature: 11.6°C (Hungary's highest)
Soils: Limestone + red clay (Terres Rouges)
Flagship wine: Villányi Franc (official certified brand)

Top Estates

Bock · Gere · Malatinszky · Vylyan

Villányi Franc vs Loire Valley Franc

CharacteristicVillányLoire Valley
ClimateWarmer, more sunshineCooler, Atlantic influence
FruitDark fruit (blackcurrant, damson)Red fruit (raspberry, red cherry)
TanninSilky, ripeFirmer, with herbal edge
Green characterAbsent — fully ripeOften a touch of green pepper
Style comparisonCloser to Right Bank BordeauxLighter, more aromatic
slides.4.title: Other Important Red Grape Varieties
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Zweigelt
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Austria's most widely planted red grape, with 2,400+ hectares in Hungary — mainly in Sopron — celebrated for its easy-drinking red-fruit style
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Portugieser
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Despite the Portuguese-sounding name, it is a Central European variety — in Villány it produces light, fresh wines that are the archetype of easy-drinking reds
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Pinot Noir
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Cultivated experimentally in Hungary's cooler regions (Eger, Sopron), but quality has not yet reached the level of Bordeaux varieties here
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Merlot / Cabernet Sauvignon
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Bordeaux varieties are also grown in Villány and Szekszárd, typically used in top-quality blends
slides.4.content:
Hungary's red wine landscape is far richer than Kékfrankos and Kadarka alone — a diverse supporting cast of international and local varieties rounds out the country's red wine offer.

Red Variety Quick Reference

VarietyKey RegionStyleArea
KékfrankosSopron · Eger · VillányDark fruit, spice, high acidity8,000+ ha
KadarkaSzekszárd · EgerRose, spice, low tannin<700 ha
Cabernet FrancVillányBlackcurrant, violet, silky tannin1,200+ ha
ZweigeltSopronRed fruit, easy-drinking, round2,400+ ha
PortugieserVillányLight, fresh, early-drinking1,000+ ha

Key Takeaway

  • Most planted: Kékfrankos (the versatile national red)
  • Most traditional: Kadarka (the aromatic soul of Bull's Blood)
  • Most international: Cabernet Franc (finding its natural home in Villány)
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
What is Kékfrankos called in Austria?
A. Kadarka
B. Zweigelt
C. Blaufränkisch
D. Portugieser

Kékfrankos is the Hungarian name for the variety known as Blaufränkisch in Austria and Lemberger in Germany. It is one of Central Europe's most important red varieties, and Hungary's Sopron region — bordering Austria — produces a style most similar to the Austrian expression.
What is the origin of the name "Bull's Blood" (Bikavér)?
A. The wine is made from a blend that includes bull's blood
B. During the 1552 siege of Eger, Ottoman soldiers saw wine staining the defenders' beards and believed they were drinking bull's blood
C. The wine's deep red colour resembles that of bull's blood
D. A famous bull breeder in Eger first popularised the wine

According to legend, during the 1552 Ottoman siege of Eger, Hungarian soldiers drank Kadarka-based wine to fuel their courage. The red wine stained their beards, and when the Ottomans spotted this, they believed the defenders were drinking bull's blood — and retreated in fear. Whether or not the story is true, it gave Hungary's most famous red blend its unforgettable name.
Which region is most celebrated for Cabernet Franc, possessing its own AOC brand "Villányi Franc"?
A. Tokaj
B. Eger
C. Villány
D. Sopron

Villány, in Hungary's far south, is the country's warmest wine region and the undisputed home of Hungarian Cabernet Franc. Its unique combination of limestone and red clay (Terres Rouges) soils, high sunshine hours and minimal spring frost risk allows Cab. Franc to achieve outstanding ripeness. British critic Michael Broadbent famously declared that the variety has "found its natural home" in Villány.
What is Kadarka's current situation in Hungary?
A. It is Hungary's most widely planted red variety with over 8,000 hectares
B. Difficult to cultivate and nearly eliminated during the communist era, it now covers fewer than 700 hectares — but is being rediscovered by boutique winemakers
C. It has completely disappeared and is no longer grown commercially
D. It is primarily found in Villány, where it is used to produce Hungary's finest red wines

Kadarka's sensitivity to spring frosts and its tendency to produce inconsistent yields made it difficult to manage under the communist collective farm system, where it was largely replaced by the more reliable Kékfrankos. Today fewer than 700 hectares remain, mainly in Szekszárd and Eger. However, a new wave of quality-focused winemakers is reviving Kadarka, releasing single-variety bottlings that reveal its unique rose-and-spice aromatic charm.
